mainEntity.name: Can I still have a dental implant if my previous root canal failed?

acceptedAnswer.text: In many cases, yes — a failed root canal does not automatically rule out future implant treatment. However, the site must be properly assessed first. Your dental team will use X-rays and a clinical examination to evaluate the bone quality and check for any residual infection. Where the bone has been affected, preparatory procedures such as infection clearance or bone grafting may be recommended before implant placement proceeds. Each case is individual, and suitability is determined through a clinical assessment rather than a general rule.

mainEntity.name: How long should I wait after a tooth extraction before having an implant placed?

acceptedAnswer.text: This depends significantly on the reason for the extraction and the condition of the site. Where an infection was present, most dental teams will allow a healing period — often three to six months — to ensure the bone has recovered adequately. In some cases with favourable conditions, immediate or early implant placement may be discussed. Where bone grafting is needed, the timeline may be longer. Your dental team will advise you on the most appropriate timing based on your specific clinical situation.

mainEntity.name: What is peri-implantitis and is it linked to previous infection?

acceptedAnswer.text: Peri-implantitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the gum and bone surrounding a dental implant, comparable in some ways to gum disease around natural teeth. It can lead to bone loss and, in advanced cases, implant failure. Some research suggests that placing implants into sites with residual infection or inadequately healed bone may increase the risk of peri-implantitis. This is one of the key reasons why thorough pre-implant assessment of previously infected sites is so important. Good oral hygiene and regular professional maintenance are essential for long-term implant health.

mainEntity.name: Is it possible to have a dental implant at a site where I had an abscess?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, it may be possible, but the site must be fully assessed and any active or residual infection must be resolved before implant placement. A dental abscess can cause significant localised bone loss, so the volume and quality of remaining bone will need to be carefully evaluated. Bone grafting may be required as a preparatory step. With appropriate planning and treatment, many patients who have experienced dental abscesses go on to have successful implant outcomes. Treatment suitability is determined on an individual basis during a clinical consultation.

mainEntity.name: Will my dentist be able to tell from an X-ray if there is still infection at an old root canal site?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental X-rays — particularly periapical X-rays and cone beam CT scans — can reveal important information about bone changes around a previous root canal site, such as dark shadow areas indicating a periapical lesion or bone resorption. However, X-rays show structural changes and not bacteria directly. A clinical examination alongside imaging provides the most complete picture. Some sites may appear radiographically normal yet show signs of ongoing inflammation clinically, which is why both elements of assessment are important.

mainEntity.name: Does everyone who has had a root canal need bone grafting before an implant?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — bone grafting is not automatically required for all patients with a root canal history. Many patients who have had successful root canal treatment, with no signs of residual infection or significant bone loss, may be suitable for straightforward implant placement without preparatory grafting. The need for bone grafting is determined by the individual clinical findings at the time of assessment, particularly the bone volume and density at the specific implant site. Your dental team will advise you accordingly following a thorough examination.
